    Fitting a Model and Checking the Fit

    Last updated on 2026-11-24 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I fit a model, and how do I know the fit worked?
    • What should I do when a check fails?

    Objectives

    • Fit any model in the lesson with fit_model().
    • Use the four checks to tell whether a fit can be used.
    • Identify the cause of a failed fit from its checks or error message, using the troubleshooting table.

    Starting Point

    This episode opens steps 3 and 4 of the Quick Start: fitting and checking.

    Prerequisite

    Run This Only If You Are Starting Here

    If you have followed along in stellako.R, you already have these objects: skip this chunk. If you are starting here or have restarted R, run this chunk first. It needs data/sockeye.csv and files/cookbook.R in your project (see Setup).

    R 

    library(RTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
source("files/cookbook.R")        # the finished recipe box (your my-recipes.R works too)
sockeye  <- read.csv("data/sockeye.csv")
my_stock <- filter(sockeye, stock == "Stellako")
dat      <- make_dat(my_stock, S_new = 50)

    What Fitting Does

    Fitting a model means finding the parameter values that make the negative log-likelihood, the surprise score of Episode 3, as small as possible. As in step 4 of the Quick Start, picture the score as the height of the ground in a valley. Each spot in the valley is one set of parameter values, and the lowest spot is the best fit.

    The optimiser, nlminb(), is a hiker in fog. It cannot see the bottom of the valley. It can only feel the slope of the ground under its feet, and it walks downhill until the ground is level. obj$fn() gives the height of the ground at any spot, and obj$gr() gives the exact slope there; statisticians call this slope the gradient.

    Here are the three calls from step 3 of the Quick Start, with the starting values from Episode 3:

    R 

    obj <- MakeADFun(function(p) nll_ricker(p, dat), start_ricker(dat), silent = TRUE)
opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr)
sdr <- sdreport(obj)
opt[c("par", "objective", "convergence", "iterations", "message")]

    OUTPUT 

    $par
 log_alpha   log_Smax  log_sigma
 2.3797073  4.8081068 -0.1199054

$objective
[1] 96.12848

$convergence
[1] 0

$iterations
[1] 14

$message
[1] "relative convergence (4)"

    The output of nlminb() is a list. Read it one element at a time:

    • par holds the best values the hiker found, on the log scale: log_alpha 2.38, log_Smax 4.81 and log_sigma -0.12. Episode 5 turns them into estimates with units and intervals.
    • objective is the negative log-likelihood at those values: 96.1, down from 144.8 at the starting values (Episode 3).
    • convergence is 0, which means the optimiser stopped normally. It does not tell you whether it stopped in a good place.
    • iterations is the number of steps downhill: 14.
    • message says why the hiker stopped: “relative convergence (4)” means further steps would make the score smaller by only a negligible amount.

    sdreport() then measures how sharply the ground curves at the bottom. A narrow, steep bowl means the data pin the parameters down, and gives small standard errors; a wide, shallow bowl gives large ones.

    In a workshop, skip the optional spoilers “How RTMB Gets Exact Slopes” (below) and “Why Restart Once?”; learners can read them later. Show the data-copy spoiler from the page without typing it: it answers misconception M11, that changing dat after a fit is harmless. If your learners rarely write functions, type fit_model() in two passes: first the three calls and a list of obj, opt and sdr, which you run; then the safety steps and the recipe items, naming each one as you add it.

    RTMB records your calculation once and works out exact slopes from the recording. This is called automatic differentiation. It is why RTMB is fast, and why your function must not use if() on a parameter: the recording follows one path only, and RTMB stops with the error Comparison is generally unsafe for AD types. To switch between models, write a separate function for each.

    Recipe: Fit Any Model

    Use it when: you fit any model, from now on.

    Ingredients: a negative log-likelihood function, starting values, a data list, and the names of any random effects.

    fit_model() packages the three calls you already know into one function. If you ran the Starting Point chunk, it is already loaded from cookbook.R; type it anyway, so that you know what it does.

    R 

    fit_model <- function(nll, par, dat, random = NULL) {
  obj <- MakeADFun(function(p) nll(p, dat), par, random = random, silent = TRUE)
  if (!is.finite(obj$fn(obj$par)))
    stop("The negative log-likelihood is not a finite number at the starting values.")
  control <- list(eval.max = 10000, iter.max = 10000)
  opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, control = control)
  opt <- nlminb(opt$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, control = control)   # restart once where it stopped
  sdr <- sdreport(obj)
  list(obj = obj, opt = opt, sdr = sdr, checks = check_fit(opt, sdr),
       nll = nll, par = par, dat = dat, random = random)       # the recipe, kept for refits
}

    These are the three calls from the Quick Start, plus four safety steps:

    • it stops with a clear message if the negative log-likelihood is not a finite number (for example NA or Inf) at the starting values;
    • it allows the optimiser more steps (10 000 instead of the default 200 evaluations and 150 iterations);
    • it restarts the optimiser once, from where it stopped;
    • it keeps the data and the recipe (the function, starting values and random effects), so that results computed after fitting use the data the model was fitted to, and later refits (Episodes 8 and 11) reuse the same recipe.

    Its last line runs check_fit(), which you typed in step 4 of the Quick Start, to get the four checks; the next section explains them. Here it is again. You do not need to type it a second time, but copy it and run it, so that fit_model() can find it even if you have restarted R since the Quick Start:

    R 

    check_fit <- function(opt, sdr) {
  c(finished  = opt$convergence == 0,                         # the optimiser stopped normally
    flat      = max(abs(sdr$gradient.fixed)) < 0.001,         # the ground is level
    curved    = sdr$pdHess,                                   # the bottom is a bowl
    finite_se = all(is.finite(summary(sdr, "fixed")[, "Std. Error"])))  # every SE is a number
}

    Now fit the Ricker model with fit_model():

    R 

    ricker <- fit_model(nll_ricker, start_ricker(dat), dat)
ricker$checks

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE

    R 

    names(ricker)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "obj"    "opt"    "sdr"    "checks" "nll"    "par"    "dat"    "random"

    ricker is a fitted model: a list that holds the three RTMB objects (obj, opt and sdr), the four checks, and the recipe it was fitted with. From now on, every model in the lesson is fitted this way.

    Check it worked: ricker$checks shows four TRUE. Put up a green sticky note when it does.

    Ask for sticky notes when ricker$checks shows four TRUE. If a learner’s own fit_model() gives an error, rerunning the Starting Point chunk loads the version in cookbook.R; fix their copy at the break. Then ask for a show of hands on the prediction below before you run rbind() (1 minute). Across all 19 stocks, a single nlminb() call already passes every check for these models, so the restart is insurance for larger models and learners’ own data, not a fix for these data.

    fit_model() runs nlminb() twice. Will its estimates differ from opt$par, which the three calls found at the start of this episode? Write down your prediction, then run:

    R 

    rbind(three_calls = opt$par, fit_model = ricker$opt$par)

    OUTPUT 

                log_alpha log_Smax  log_sigma
three_calls  2.379707 4.808107 -0.1199054
fit_model    2.379707 4.808107 -0.1199054

    The two rows are identical. For these data, one run of nlminb() already reached the bottom, so the restart found nothing to improve.

    nlminb() sometimes stops a little short of the bottom in larger models. Starting it again from where it stopped costs little: a few milliseconds for the models in this lesson. For every single-stock fit in this lesson, one run was already enough.

    RTMB reruns your R function after fitting when it computes reported quantities such as mu_new (and their standard errors), residuals and simulations. A model built with the raw calls reads dat from your workspace each time, so editing dat after fitting changes those results without any warning. This chunk changes S_new after a fit made with the raw calls:

    R 

    dat_demo <- dat
obj_demo <- MakeADFun(function(p) nll_ricker(p, dat_demo), start_ricker(dat_demo), silent = TRUE)
opt_demo <- nlminb(obj_demo$par, obj_demo$fn, obj_demo$gr)
dat_demo$S_new <- 150                    # change the data after fitting
summary(sdreport(obj_demo), "report")    # mu_new now silently uses S_new = 150

    OUTPUT 

           Estimate Std. Error
mu_new 1.155212  0.2328307

    R 

    summary(ricker$sdr, "report")            # fit_model() kept its copy: S_new = 50

    OUTPUT 

           Estimate Std. Error
mu_new 1.971542  0.1035622

    The forecast mu_new from the raw calls is now 1.16, the value for 150 thousand spawners, although the model was fitted when S_new was 50. The fitted model from fit_model() still gives 1.97, the value for 50 thousand spawners. fit_model() gives each model its own copy of the data; to change the data, fit the model again.

    The Four Checks

    A fit can be used only when all four checks are TRUE. Each line of check_fit() asks one question:

    • finished reads the optimiser’s convergence code.
    • flat asks whether every slope (gradient.fixed) is close to zero where the hiker stopped.
    • curved reads pdHess (short for “positive definite Hessian”), which is TRUE when the curvature at the bottom, called the Hessian, forms a bowl.
    • finite_se asks whether every standard error is a number, not NaN (not a number) or Inf (infinity).
    The four checks, and what a failure usually means.
    Check Question In the picture A failure usually means
    finished Did the optimiser stop normally? the hiker stopped walking it hit a limit or ran away: a model error (Challenge 3) or a missing random =
    flat Is the ground level where it stopped? flat ground underfoot it stopped early, or the score has no bottom (Challenge 1)
    curved Is the bottom a bowl? one lowest spot two parameters do one job, or the data cannot pin one down
    finite_se Can every standard error be computed? the width of the bowl can be measured as for curved

    Four TRUE say that the hiker stands at the bottom of a bowl. They cannot say whether a lower bowl exists elsewhere in the valley; starting values taken from the data make stopping in the wrong bowl less likely.

    When a Check Fails

    A fit can fail without any error from R. The next challenge shows a fit that looks finished but cannot be used.

    Make the sign error live: type nll_sign, fit it, and let learners read the output before you explain anything. A mistake made in front of the room is a teaching moment. Then ask the question below and let learners vote. If most choose (a), they think that convergence == 0 means a usable fit (misconception M2): show m_sign$opt$par, ask what S_max would be, and repeat that code 0 only says the optimiser stopped. If answers are spread out, go back to the valley picture and the four checks. The demonstration and the vote take about 5 minutes.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Is This Fit Usable? (3 minutes)

    Someone wrote this model and fitted it to the Stellako data:

    R 

    nll_sign <- function(par, dat) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)
  mu <- log_alpha - S / exp(log_Smax)
  sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, exp(log_sigma), log = TRUE))
}
m_sign <- fit_model(nll_sign, start_ricker(dat), dat)
m_sign$opt[c("objective", "convergence", "message")]
m_sign$checks

    R printed two warnings, NA/NaN function evaluation, and then:

    OUTPUT 

    $objective
[1] -Inf

$convergence
[1] 0

$message
[1] "X-convergence (3)"

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE     FALSE     FALSE     FALSE

    Is this fit usable?

    • (a) Yes: convergence is 0.
    • (b) No: three of the four checks fail.
    • (c) Yes, if the estimates look reasonable.
    • (d) No, because the message is not “relative convergence”.

    The answer is (b).

    R 

    nll_sign <- function(par, dat) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)
  mu <- log_alpha - S / exp(log_Smax)
  sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, exp(log_sigma), log = TRUE))   # minus sign missing
}
m_sign <- fit_model(nll_sign, start_ricker(dat), dat)

    WARNING 

    Warning in nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, control = control): NA/NaN function
evaluation

    WARNING 

    Warning in nlminb(opt$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, control = control): NA/NaN function
evaluation

    R 

    m_sign$opt[c("objective", "convergence", "message")]

    OUTPUT 

    $objective
[1] -Inf

$convergence
[1] 0

$message
[1] "X-convergence (3)"

    R 

    m_sign$checks

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE     FALSE     FALSE     FALSE

    R 

    m_sign$opt$par

    OUTPUT 

       log_alpha     log_Smax    log_sigma
   0.7471605 -176.0607325 -180.3133672

    The two warnings, NA/NaN function evaluation, come from the two runs of nlminb(): the optimiser tried values where the score could not be computed.

    • (a) is the most common mistake: convergence code 0 only says that the optimiser stopped, not that it stopped at a sensible bottom.
    • (b) is right. The cause is the missing minus sign: the function returns the log-likelihood, and the optimiser makes it as small as possible, so it runs off to minus infinity. The ground is not flat there, and there is no bowl.
    • (c) is wrong twice. The estimates are absurd: log_Smax is about -176, so S_max would be exp(-176) thousand spawners, far less than one fish. (The exact value depends on your computer, because this score has no bottom; it is always a huge negative number.) And judging estimates by eye is not a test; the four checks are.
    • (d) is the right verdict for the wrong reason. The wording of the message is not the test: usable fits can also stop with other messages.
    Caution

    Convergence Code 0 Is Not Enough

    opt$convergence can be 0 for a fit that is useless, as in Challenge 1. Use all four checks.

    Whether a check fails or fit_model() stops with an error, first look up the pattern of checks and messages in the Troubleshooting table. It lists the mistakes in the code, such as a missing minus sign, a missing log = TRUE or a missing random =, and the pattern each one leaves. If no row matches, work down these five questions; they find problems in the data, the scales and the starting values.

    Checklist

    When a Check Fails, Work Down This List

    1. Is obj$fn(obj$par) a finite number? (fit_model() stops if not.)
    2. Look at the data: missing values, zeros, units.
    3. Are positive parameters on the log scale?
    4. Do the starting values come from the data?
    5. Simplify: remove a parameter the data cannot inform.
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Diagnose Three Fits (8 minutes)

    Here are the outputs of three failed fits, all to the Stellako data (74 brood years). Match each output to its cause, using the table of the four checks above and the Troubleshooting page. Two causes are not used.

    1. log = TRUE missing in dnorm().
    2. random = missing in a model with random effects.
    3. Two parameters that do the same job.
    4. A missing value (NA) in the data.
    5. The minus sign missing.

    Output A shows m$checks, m$opt$message and the number of estimated parameters, length(m$opt$par):

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
    FALSE     FALSE     FALSE     FALSE

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "false convergence (8)"

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 79

    Output B shows m$checks and summary(m$sdr, "fixed"):

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE     FALSE     FALSE

    OUTPUT 

                Estimate Std. Error
log_alpha  2.1576015        NaN
log_Smax   4.8081069        NaN
log_sigma -0.1199050        NaN
log_extra  0.2221058        NaN

    Output C is an error:

    ERROR 

    Error in `fit_model()`:
! The negative log-likelihood is not a finite number at the starting values.

    Count the parameters in Output A. The Ricker has three. The random walk from step 7 of the Quick Start has four fixed parameters; its 75 yearly productivities are kept out of opt$par only when they are named in random =.

    A matches 2, B matches 3 and C matches 4.

    A: random = missing. The random-walk model from the Quick Start, fitted without random = "log_alpha_year", estimates all 75 yearly productivities as ordinary fixed parameters: 79 parameters in all. (start_walk() comes from cookbook.R; Episode 6 teaches it. Episode 3 did not load cookbook.R, so if R cannot find start_walk() or nll_walk, run source("files/cookbook.R") first.)

    R 

    m_a <- fit_model(nll_walk, start_walk(dat), dat)
m_a$checks

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
    FALSE     FALSE     FALSE     FALSE

    R 

    m_a$opt$message

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "false convergence (8)"

    R 

    length(m_a$opt$par)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 79

    R 

    range(m_a$opt$par[-(1:4)])          # the 75 yearly values: lowest and highest

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 2.114435 2.114435

    R 

    exp(m_a$opt$par[["log_sd_walk"]])   # sd_walk, the size of the yearly steps

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 6.231478e-15

    R 

    m_a$opt$objective

    OUTPUT 

    [1] -1950.661

    Without random =, the optimiser chooses every yearly value itself. It makes all 75 of them the same (about 2.1 on the log scale), so every yearly step is zero, and then shrinks the size of the steps towards zero: sd_walk collapses to about 6e-15 and the score runs down to -1951. The score has no bottom, so all four checks fail; the exact numbers depend on your computer, because the optimiser stops wherever it gives up. The 79 parameters are the clue: the random walk has four fixed parameters, so a correct fit reports four. The fix is to name the random effects:

    R 

    m_a_fixed <- fit_model(nll_walk, start_walk(dat), dat, random = "log_alpha_year")
m_a_fixed$checks

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE

    R 

    length(m_a_fixed$opt$par)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 4

    B: two parameters that do the same job.

    R 

    nll_two <- function(par, dat) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)
  mu <- log_alpha + log_extra - S / exp(log_Smax)     # two parameters doing one job
  -sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, exp(log_sigma), log = TRUE))
}
m_b <- fit_model(nll_two, c(start_ricker(dat), list(log_extra = 0)), dat)
m_b$checks

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE     FALSE     FALSE

    R 

    summary(m_b$sdr, "fixed")

    OUTPUT 

                Estimate Std. Error
log_alpha  2.1576015        NaN
log_Smax   4.8081069        NaN
log_sigma -0.1199050        NaN
log_extra  0.2221058        NaN

    log_alpha and log_extra add up to 2.38, the Ricker’s log_alpha, but the data can only tell their sum. Any split between them fits equally well: the valley has a long flat floor, so the standard errors cannot be computed. curved is FALSE here, but in fits like this it can also come out TRUE, depending on the computer: trust finite_se. The fix is to remove log_extra: the model is then the Ricker, which passes all four checks (ricker$checks above).

    C: a missing value in the data.

    R 

    dat_na <- dat
dat_na$logRS[5] <- NA
fit_model(nll_ricker, start_ricker(dat_na), dat_na)

    ERROR 

    Error in `fit_model()`:
! The negative log-likelihood is not a finite number at the starting values.

    One NA in logRS makes the whole score NA, so fit_model() stops before the optimiser starts. The fix is to remove the rows with missing values from the data frame before make_dat(), for example with filter(my_stock, !is.na(spawners), !is.na(recruits)).

    The unused causes: a missing minus sign (5) gives TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE and a score of -Inf, as in Challenge 1. A missing log = TRUE (1) also gives four FALSE, but with a different message and only three parameters; you will meet it in Challenge 3.

    Give learners 5 minutes alone, then 3 minutes to compare answers with a neighbour. If many match A with cause 1 (log = TRUE missing), point at the 79: the number of estimated parameters is the clue that the random effects were not declared. Cause 3 is the hardest to picture; draw the flat-bottomed trough from the figure.

    Reading Error Messages

    When R stops with an error, read the message from the bottom up. The last line says what went wrong: look it up in the table below. The first line usually says where R stopped, for example Error in fit_model(nll_ricker, start_ricker(dat_na), dat_na) : for Output C of Challenge 2. An error inside your model function starts with Error in nll(p, dat) :, because nll is the name fit_model() gives your function. (This page, and some editors, show errors in a slightly different layout.)

    Most problems with fitting come from a small set of mistakes in the model function. The table lists the five most common (m is any fitted model); the Troubleshooting page lists every message this lesson produces.

    Caution

    Common Problems: Fit Any Model

    The five most common problems when fitting a model.
    What you see Likely cause Fix
    object 'logRS' not found or object 'log_alpha' not found (a name from dat or par) getAll(par, dat) is missing make it the first line of the function
    object 'log_S_max' not found a name differs between the function and par or dat compare the names letter by letter
    Comparison is generally unsafe for AD types if() on a parameter remove it; write a separate model function for each case
    checks TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE, m$opt$objective is -Inf, “X-convergence (3)” the function returns the log-likelihood put a minus sign in front of sum()
    all four checks FALSE, “function evaluation limit reached without convergence (9)” log = TRUE missing in dnorm() add it
    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Find the Bug (6 minutes)

    This model was fitted to the Stellako data:

    R 

    nll_nolog <- function(par, dat) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)
  mu <- log_alpha - S / exp(log_Smax)
  -sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, exp(log_sigma)))
}
m_nolog <- fit_model(nll_nolog, start_ricker(dat), dat)
m_nolog$opt$message
m_nolog$opt$par
m_nolog$checks

    R printed There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first 50), and then:

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "function evaluation limit reached without convergence (9)"

    OUTPUT 

      log_alpha    log_Smax   log_sigma
   2.398421    5.466528 -666.201828

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
    FALSE     FALSE     FALSE     FALSE

    Use the table above to find the likely cause. Which line is wrong? Copy the code from this page rather than typing it, then fix the function and refit.

    The last line is wrong: log = TRUE is missing in dnorm(). This chunk reruns the broken fit; suppressWarnings() hides its 10 000 copies of the warning NA/NaN function evaluation. We hide the warnings only to keep this page short; in your own work, read them.

    R 

    nll_nolog <- function(par, dat) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)
  mu <- log_alpha - S / exp(log_Smax)
  -sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, exp(log_sigma)))
}
m_nolog <- suppressWarnings(fit_model(nll_nolog, start_ricker(dat), dat))
m_nolog$opt$message

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "function evaluation limit reached without convergence (9)"

    R 

    m_nolog$opt$par

    OUTPUT 

      log_alpha    log_Smax   log_sigma
   2.398421    5.466528 -666.201828

    R 

    m_nolog$checks

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
    FALSE     FALSE     FALSE     FALSE

    Without log = TRUE, dnorm() returns densities, and the function adds them up instead of adding log-densities. When the curve passes through one point exactly, that point’s density grows without limit as sigma shrinks towards zero, so the score has no bottom. The first run of nlminb() walked downhill until log_sigma reached -666 (the exact value depends on your computer), and stopped there. The restart then tried 10 000 times to take one more step, but the score could not be computed at any of the new values it tried, so nearly every try printed a warning. It stopped at its limit of 10 000 evaluations without moving, so finished is FALSE.

    Add log = TRUE and refit:

    R 

    nll_fixed <- function(par, dat) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)
  mu <- log_alpha - S / exp(log_Smax)
  -sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, exp(log_sigma), log = TRUE))   # log = TRUE added
}
m_fixed <- fit_model(nll_fixed, start_ricker(dat), dat)
m_fixed$checks

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE

    R 

    m_fixed$opt$par

    OUTPUT 

     log_alpha   log_Smax  log_sigma
 2.3797073  4.8081068 -0.1199054

    All four checks are TRUE, and the estimates are the Ricker’s: 2.38, 4.81 and -0.12.

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: Your Turn: Upper Pitt River, Row 2 (8 minutes)

    Fit the Ricker model to Upper Pitt River with fit_model(). Use the names pitt, dat_pitt and ricker_pitt, so that the Stellako objects stay as they are. Add the code to upper-pitt-river.R and record its checks in row 2 of your report card, as a comment line under it. Put up a green sticky note when ricker_pitt$checks shows four TRUE.

    pitt and dat_pitt are in upper-pitt-river.R from Episode 3 (Challenge 5); if they are not in your workspace, run the script from the top. Then copy the line that fitted ricker above, ricker <- fit_model(nll_ricker, start_ricker(dat), dat), and change ricker to ricker_pitt and each dat to dat_pitt.

    R 

    pitt        <- filter(sockeye, stock == "Upper Pitt River")
dat_pitt    <- make_dat(pitt, S_new = mean(tail(pitt$spawners, 4)))
ricker_pitt <- fit_model(nll_ricker, start_ricker(dat_pitt), dat_pitt)
ricker_pitt$checks

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE

    All four checks are TRUE, so the fit can be used.

    Row 2: “Ricker: all four checks TRUE.” (Other models are added in Episodes 6 and 9.) In upper-pitt-river.R, add the two ricker_pitt lines (the first two lines of the chunk are already there from Episode 3), then the row comment # Row 2 (fits usable): Ricker: all four checks TRUE.

    Check that learners named the fit ricker_pitt. Anyone who overwrote ricker should run ricker <- fit_model(nll_ricker, start_ricker(dat), dat) again before Episode 5, which uses the Stellako fit.

    Callout

    Add to Your Recipe Box

    Copy these functions into your my-recipes.R: fit_model(), and check_fit() from the Quick Start, which fit_model() uses. The finished box is cookbook.R.

    Callout

    In Your Field

    The four checks apply to any model fitted by maximum likelihood. glmmTMB and TMB report the same quantities: convergence, the gradient, whether the Hessian is positive definite (the curved check), and the standard errors.

    Key Points

    • fit_model() builds a model with MakeADFun(), fits it with nlminb() (restarting once), computes standard errors with sdreport(), and keeps the data and recipe it used.
    • A fit can be used only when all four checks are TRUE: finished, flat, curved and finite_se.
    • convergence == 0 on its own is not evidence of a usable fit.
    • When a check fails or R stops, look up the symptom in the troubleshooting table; if no row matches, work through the list: a finite start, the data, the log scale for positive parameters, the starting values, a simpler model.
